concept.title: Optical signs come from declared directions
concept.inferential_jump: The Cartesian sign convention turns a mirror diagram into signed distances and heights; the signs come from declared directions, not from memorized object/image labels.
entry_assumptions: R2: image nature is determined by actual versus backward-extended ray intersection.

teaching_path.action: Mark the pole as the distance origin, declare the direction of incident light as the positive horizontal direction, and declare upward from the principal axis as positive height.
teaching_path.why_valid: Signs can only be reproducible when the origin and positive directions are fixed before any object or image is classified.
teaching_path.output: pole = origin; incident-light direction = positive distance; upward = positive height

teaching_path.action: Take several marked points and assign each a distance sign from the pole and a height sign from the principal axis using only the declared directions.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same coordinate rule applies to every point, so the result cannot depend on whether a point is called object, image, center or another label.
teaching_path.output: with incident direction -> positive distance; against it -> negative distance; above axis -> positive height; below -> negative height

teaching_path.action: Redraw the same physical setup reversed left-to-right on the page, carrying the declared incident-light arrow with it, and assign the signs again.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct convention follows the declared physical direction, so changing the page layout does not change the signs of the same physical quantities.
teaching_path.output: page reversed + direction declaration carried with setup -> physical sign assignments preserved

predict.prompt: If the same mirror setup is drawn on the opposite side of the page, should an object's sign change merely because its ink moved left or right?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The sign follows the declared incident-light and vertical directions, which move with the physical setup rather than staying attached to page left or page right.

attempt.produces: A sign-labelled mirror sketch with origin and positive directions declared before any object, image or focal-location signs are assigned.

rubric.criterion: The pole and both positive directions are declared before signs are written.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the coordinate convention as the source of the signs.

rubric.criterion: Every longitudinal and vertical sign is justified by direction from the declared reference.
rubric.evidence_of: Avoiding memorized sign rules tied to object or image labels.

accepted: The sketch marks the pole, incident-light arrow and upward direction first, then gives each position and height a sign by comparing it with those declarations.
rejected: The response writes object is negative and image is positive before declaring any direction, so the signs are attached to labels rather than coordinates.

route.ask: Before assigning any sign, where is the distance origin in this diagram?
route.why_this_ask: A sign without an origin is not a coordinate decision.

route.ask: Which physical direction has been declared positive for longitudinal distance, and which for height?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must state both coordinate directions before classifying points.

route.ask: Take one point without calling it object or image. Which sign follows from its direction from the pole?
route.why_this_ask: Removing the familiar label tests whether the coordinate rule can stand on its own.

route.ask: If the page drawing is reversed, what must move with the setup so your signs remain physically consistent?
route.why_this_ask: The reversal exposes page-left or page-right memorization.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path declares a full coordinate system first; the elicitation route removes object and image labels and makes the learner recover signs from an unlabeled point before testing a mirrored page layout.

boundary_test.prompt: What sign should a point exactly at the pole have for its longitudinal distance?
boundary_test.answer: Its distance is zero, so it is neither on the positive nor negative side of the origin.
boundary_test.confirms: The sign convention is a coordinate system with an origin, not a permanent label attached to a class of optical object.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Object distance is always negative and image distance is always positive.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Move the same object-and-mirror sketch so incident light travels the opposite page direction. Should the sign rule follow the page or the declared incident-light direction?
misconceptions.repair: Apply the coordinate convention from the pole every time; signs follow measurement direction and height orientation.

exit_task.prompt: A mirror diagram declares its pole, incident-light direction and upward direction. Assign signs to the object distance, image distance, focal-location distance and image height from those declarations, and explain why an object-or-image sign table was unnecessary.

answer.summary: Each sign follows the declared coordinate direction from the pole or principal axis; the labels object and image do not determine signs by themselves.
reasoning: Use the pole as the horizontal origin and compare every longitudinal position with the declared incident-light direction.
Use the principal axis as the vertical reference and compare each height with the declared upward direction.
Apply those two rules consistently to every named point instead of switching rules when the label changes.
answer.check: Mirror the whole drawing left-to-right while carrying the incident-light arrow with the physical setup; a convention-based answer should remain physically consistent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer assigns qualitative signs from a declared coordinate convention and computes no numerical optical result.
